units.name: glob-matching
units.role: Compile shell-style glob patterns and test paths against them.
units.description: This unit is the glob pattern engine used throughout the tool. It understands shell-style wildcard patterns like `*.rs` or `src/**/foo.rs`, turning them into compiled matchers that can quickly answer 'does this file path match this pattern?' It can also hold many patterns at once (a 'glob set') and, given a path, report every pattern that matches. This is the building block other parts of the program use to decide which files to include or exclude, but this unit itself never touches the filesystem, network, or any other outside resource — it is a pure, self-contained pattern-matching library.

units.name: ignore-and-walk
units.role: Walk a directory tree, applying gitignore-style rules to decide what to skip.
units.description: This is the engine that decides which files and folders ripgrep should actually look inside when you run a search. It walks through a directory tree (optionally using multiple threads for speed), while reading and applying the same kind of exclusion rules Git uses (.gitignore, .ignore, global git excludes, .git/info/exclude, and custom rules like ripgrep's own overrides and file-type filters such as 'only search *.rs files'). It relies on the separate glob-matching unit to actually test file names against wildcard patterns, and it talks directly to the operating system's filesystem (and to git's configuration files) to figure out what exists and what should be skipped.

units.name: matcher-contract
units.role: Define the shared interface every pattern-matching engine implements.
units.description: This is the shared rulebook that all of ripgrep's different search engines agree to follow. It defines what a 'match' looks like (a start and end position in text), what a 'line ending' is, how to report multiple matches or none at all, and how to fill in capture groups when doing find-and-replace. It doesn't itself search anything or read any files — it's just the agreed-upon interface, like a contract, that the Rust-regex engine and the PCRE2 engine both promise to implement, so the rest of ripgrep can work with either one interchangeably.

units.name: regex-engine
units.role: Adapt Rust's regex library to the matcher contract, with literal extraction and safety checks.
units.description: This unit takes a regular expression pattern typed by a user and turns it into a ready-to-use pattern matcher that the rest of ripgrep can call to find matches in text. It leans on Rust's external regex libraries to do the actual pattern matching, but adds intelligence on top: deciding when a search should ignore letter case, making sure a pattern can never accidentally match across a line boundary, pulling out short literal snippets from a pattern so ripgrep can skip most of a file quickly before running the full pattern, and rejecting patterns that would be dangerous or impossible to satisfy. It also turns errors from the underlying regex library into ripgrep's own, more user-friendly error type.

units.name: pcre2-engine
units.role: Adapt the external PCRE2 C library to the matcher contract as an alternate regex backend.
units.description: This is the piece of ripgrep that lets it use the PCRE2 regular-expression engine — a widely used C library — instead of ripgrep's own built-in Rust regex engine. It is only compiled in when ripgrep is built with the optional 'pcre2' feature, and it is what powers ripgrep's -P/--pcre2 flag, giving users access to advanced pattern features like lookaround and backreferences. It works as an adapter: it takes ripgrep's generic matching contract and implements it on top of the external PCRE2 library, translating ripgrep's options into PCRE2's own configuration.

units.name: line-searcher
units.role: Read a byte stream and find matching lines using a supplied matcher, reporting to a sink.
units.description: This is the core search engine of ripgrep: given a pattern-matching engine and a source of bytes (a file, standard input, or an in-memory slice), it reads through the data line by line — or across multiple lines when configured — finds where matches occur, and reports each match, along with any requested surrounding context lines, to whatever component is consuming the results. It also detects binary data (so searching binary files as text can be skipped), can invert a search to find non-matching lines, and can use memory-mapped files for speed. It does not itself understand regular expressions or know how to print anything to a terminal.

units.name: result-printer
units.role: Render search results found by line-searcher into human- or machine-readable output formats.
units.description: This unit is responsible for turning the raw list of things ripgrep found while searching a file into text that a person or another program can read. It knows about three output styles: the classic grep-style listing of matching lines (with optional colors and clickable file-path hyperlinks), a one-line-per-file 'summary' style, and a JSON-lines machine-readable style. It also keeps running statistics (bytes searched, matches found, elapsed time) and formats file paths and hyperlinks consistently. It does not search anything itself and does not decide what counts as a match — it only receives match information from the line-searcher unit and renders it to whatever writer the caller hands it.

units.name: cli-support
units.role: Grab-bag of real-world plumbing for building command-line search tools.
units.description: This is a toolbox of small, reusable helpers for building command-line search tools like ripgrep. It knows how to transparently decompress files by shelling out to external programs like gzip or xz; safely turn arbitrary, possibly non-UTF-8, bytes into readable escaped text and back again; look up the machine's hostname; parse human-friendly size strings like '10M' into byte counts; and create properly buffered, color-capable writers to stdout. It does not implement any searching logic itself — it exists purely to handle the messy real-world plumbing of spawning processes, reading the environment, and talking to the terminal, so the rest of the program can stay focused on search behavior.

units.name: index-engine
units.role: Build and discover an on-disk literal/ngram index used to pre-filter files before searching.
units.description: This is the code for ripgrep's experimental 'index' feature: a way to build a small on-disk database that remembers which short chunks of text (ngrams) appear in which files, so a later search can quickly skip files that could not possibly contain a match instead of reading every file. One part figures out, from a search pattern, which literal fragments would have to be present for the pattern to match. The other part manages the actual index database on disk: creating it, opening it, and finding it automatically near the current directory, similar to how a .git folder is found. This feature is off by default and only compiled in when the 'unstable-index' option is enabled, since it's still a prototype.

units.name: grep-facade
units.role: Re-export the six constituent search crates under one namespace for the ripgrep binary and library consumers.
units.description: This is a tiny connector that does not contain any real logic itself. Its only job is to gather together six separate ripgrep building-block libraries — command-line helpers, the matcher contract, the PCRE2 engine, the result printer, the regex engine, and the line searcher — and offer them all under one convenient name, so that other parts of the program (and outside programmers using ripgrep as a library) can reach any of these pieces through a single path instead of hunting down six different dependencies.

units.name: cli-flags
units.role: Define, parse and validate ripgrep's command-line flags, and generate help/man/completions.
units.description: This is ripgrep's command-line interface definition: it lists every flag and positional argument ripgrep understands, reads them off the command line (and an optional config file), turns them into a validated set of settings, and can print help text, a man page, or shell-completion scripts. In short, it is where ripgrep decides 'here is everything the user is allowed to ask for, and here is what each request means' before handing a ready-to-use settings object to the rest of the program to actually perform a search. Its central settings object is also where those settings get turned into live objects — a directory walker, a pattern matcher, an output printer — from the other units it depends on.

units.name: app-orchestration
units.role: Run one end-to-end invocation of ripgrep: walk files, search each one, print results, report the exit status.
units.description: This is the code that runs when you type `rg` at the command line and press enter. It reads the parsed command-line options, then walks through the files (or reads standard input) that need to be searched, hands each one off to the actual pattern-matching machinery, and writes the results — or an error/warning message — back out. It decides between searching one file at a time or in parallel across many threads, handles decompressing compressed files or running an external 'preprocessor' command before searching, tracks whether any errors happened so the program's exit code is correct, and prints a summary of statistics at the end if requested. It also contains ripgrep's small on/off switch for the experimental indexing feature.

violations_observed.note: HiArgs (cli-flags) constructs objects from app-orchestration's public types (HaystackBuilder, SearchWorkerBuilder, PatternMatcher) while app-orchestration's main.rs also calls into cli-flags (parse, HiArgs). This is a legitimate two-way dependency through each side's declared public entrypoints, not a reach into internals, but it means these two units are mutually coupled rather than cleanly layered — both originate from the single crates/core binary and were split along a domain seam (what can be asked vs. what actually runs) rather than an acyclic dependency seam.
